modern_osis:
Hosea — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Henry considers it probable that Hosea came from the kingdom of Israel.

Hosea lived and prophesied over a long period.

His prophecies sought to expose, rebuke and convince the Jewish people in general—and the Israelites in particular—of their many sins, especially idolatry.

He also drew attention to the corruption of the kingdom.

Yet Hosea invited the people to repent, promising mercy and announcing future gospel blessings.

Henry understands these promises to concern the restoration of Israel and Judah and their eventual conversion to Christianity.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesUnder a figure, is represented the shameful idolatry of the ten tribes.1–7The calling of the Gentiles, and the uniting Israel and Judah under the Messiah.8–11
The unfaithfulness of Israel represented (verses 1–7)

Israel was prosperous when Hosea boldly exposed its sins and predicted its destruction.

We should not flatter sinners merely because they enjoy worldly success.

That success will not continue if they persist in their wrongdoing.

The prophet had to show Israel how hateful its idolatry was.

Giving a created thing the glory belonging only to God is an offense against him.

It is like a wife giving herself to a stranger instead of remaining faithful to her husband.

The Lord surely had wise reasons for the command he gave Hosea.

The prophet's experience would provide a moving image of God's undeserved goodness and tireless patience, compared with Israel's rebellion and ingratitude.

We would become tired and bitter after enduring far less unfaithfulness from other people than the unfaithfulness with which we grieve God's Spirit.

We should be ready to bear whatever cross the Lord assigns us.

The names of Hosea's children announced the people's impending ruin.

The name of the first child, Jezreel, meaning “dispersion” according to Henry, foretold the fall of the royal family.

The second, Lo-ruhamah, meant “not loved” or “not shown mercy”, announcing that the nation would be abandoned.

God had shown Israel great mercy, but the people had abused his gifts.

Sin turns away God's mercy, even from people who profess to belong to him.

If pardoning mercy is withdrawn, no other mercy can be relied upon.

Nevertheless, although some are broken off through unbelief, God will preserve a church in the world until the end.

Our salvation comes through his mercy, not through any merit of ours.

When he undertakes to save, no one can prevent him.

God's people will be gathered (verses 8–11)

A third child was called Lo-ammi, meaning “not my people”.

The name announced Israel's temporary rejection.

God disowned the relationship the nation had claimed.

We love God because he loved us first.

But when we are cast out of covenant fellowship, our own folly is to blame.

Even in wrath, God remembers mercy.

The rejection would be neither total nor final.

The same hand that wounded the people would reach out to heal them.

Precious promises are made here concerning the Israel of God.

Henry notes that some interpreters expect their fullest realization only through a future general conversion of the Jewish people.

The apostles Paul (Romans 9:25–26) and Peter (1 Peter 2:10) also apply this promise to the gospel and to Jews and Gentiles being brought together.

To believe in Christ is to receive him as our Head, willingly submitting to his guidance and rule.

Let us pray for the glorious day when one Lord will reign over all the earth.
classic_reading:
[Hos.1.1-Hos.1.7]
Hosea
Hosea is supposed to have been of the kingdom of Israel. He lived and prophesied during a long period. The scope of his predictions appears to be, to detect, reprove, and convince the Jewish nation in general, and the Israelites in particular, of their many sins, particularly their idolatry: the corrupt state of the kingdom is also noticed. But he invites them to repentance, with promises of mercy, and gospel predictions of the future restoration of the Israelites and of the Jews, and their final conversion to Christianity.
Chapter 1
Under a figure, is represented the shameful idolatry of the ten tribes. (Hos. 1:1-7) The calling of the Gentiles, and the uniting Israel and Judah under the Messiah. (Hos. 1:8-11)
Verses 1-7 Israel was prosperous, yet then Hosea boldly tells them of their sins, and foretells their destruction. Men are not to be flattered in sinful ways because they prosper in the world; nor will it last long if they go on still in their trespasses. The prophet must show Israel their sin; show it to be exceedingly hateful. Their idolatry is the sin they are here charged with. Giving that glory to any creature which is due to God alone, is an injury and affront to God; such as for a wife to take a stranger, is to her husband. The Lord, doubtless, had good reasons for giving such a command to the prophet; it would form an affecting picture of the Lord's unmerited goodness and unwearied patience, and of the perverseness and ingratitude of Israel. We should be broken and wearied with half that perverseness from others, with which we try the patience and grieve the Spirit of our God. Let us also be ready to bear any cross the Lord appoints. The prophet must show the ruin of the people, in the names given to his children. He foretells the fall of the royal family in the name of his first child: call his name Jezreel, which signifies "dispersion." He foretells God's abandoning the nation in the name of the second child; Lo-ruhamah, "not beloved," or "not having obtained mercy." God showed great mercy, but Israel abused his favours. Sin turns away the mercy of God, even from Israel, his own professing people. If pardoning mercy is denied, no other mercy can be expected. Though some, through unbelief, are broken off, yet God will have a church in this world till the end of time. Our salvation is owing to God's mercy, not to any merit of our own. That salvation is sure, of which he is the Author; and if he will work, none shall hinder.
[Hos.1.8-Hos.1.11]
Verses 8-11 The rejection of Israel for a time, is signified by the name of another child: call him Lo-ammi, "not my people." The Lord disowns all relation to them. We love him, because he first loved us; but our being cast out of covenant, is owing to ourselves and our folly. Mercy is remembered in the midst of wrath; the rejection, as it shall not be total, so it shall not be final. The same hand that wounded, is stretched forth to heal. Very precious promises are here given concerning the Israel of God, and they may be of use to us now. Some think that these promises will not have accomplishment in full, till the general conversion of the Jews in the latter days. Also this promise is applied to the gospel, and the bringing in both the Jews and Gentiles to it, by St. Paul, Rom. 9:25,26, and by St. Peter, I Pet. 2:10. To believe in Christ, is to have him for our Head, and willingly to commit ourselves to his guidance and government. And let us pray for the coming of the glorious day, when there shall be one Lord through all the earth.

Israel is charged with unfaithfulness (verses 1–5)

This chapter continues the picture of Israel as an unfaithful wife, with Hosea's children representing the people.

We should recognize and love as brothers and sisters everyone whom the Lord appears to place among his children, encouraging them in the mercy they have received.

Yet every Christian must also oppose wrongdoing through example and conduct, even among people to whom we belong and whom we should respect.

Unrepentant sinners will eventually lose the privileges they misuse and spend upon their sinful desires.

God's discipline interrupts sinful pursuits (verses 6–13)

God warned what he would do to this unfaithful, idolatrous people.

They refused to turn back, so the promised consequences came upon them.

Their history is recorded to warn us.

If people overcome smaller obstacles in pursuing sin, God may raise up greater obstacles.

Those most determined to follow sinful paths often encounter the most frustration.

When a path is blocked by thorns, we may have reason to suspect that the path itself is wrong.

Obstacles placed in the way of sin can be great blessings.

They are God's hedges, protecting us by making wrongdoing difficult.

We should thank him for grace that restrains us and for the providential events that keep us from evil—even pain, illness or calamity, if they prevent further sin.

When created things disappoint our longing for happiness, those disappointments should lead us back to the Creator.

People who forget that their comforts come from God may discover that he removes those comforts in mercy, bringing them to recognize their folly and danger.

Sin and merriment cannot remain together indefinitely.

If people refuse to take sin away from their pleasures, God will take pleasure away from their sins.

If they destroy the honor of God's word and worship, it is just for him to destroy their vines and fig trees, taking away what makes them happy.

Removing the sacred feasts and Sabbaths may not disturb them—they already care little for such things.

But when God removes their sensual pleasures, sorrow will replace sinful celebration.

God's promises of reconciliation (verses 14–23)

After judgment, the Lord promised to deal gently with Israel.

Christ's promise of rest invites us to take his yoke upon us.

Conversion may be encouraged by comfort and kindness, not only by the conviction of sin.

Yet often God brings us to the end of confidence in earthly joy and in our own strength.

When every other door closes, we finally knock at the gate of mercy.

Israel would then love God more sincerely.

Instead of calling him Baali, “my lord and master,” emphasizing authority, the people would call him Ishi, a name expressing affection.

Henry sees possible fulfillments in the return from Babylon, Jewish conversion to Christ during the apostolic age, and a future general conversion of the Jewish nation.

Believers can expect greater tenderness and care from their holy God than a beloved wife receives from even the kindest husband.

When the people put away idols and loved the Lord, no creature would finally harm them.

These promises can be understood of spiritual Israel, of every genuine believer receiving Christ's righteousness, and of future Jewish conversion.

There is also a call to live in a way that does not disgrace the God who says “You are my people.”

A household behaving shamefully dishonors its head.

If God calls us his children, let us respond, “You are our God.”

Discouraged sinner, do not answer God's love with unbelief.

When he says, “You are my people,” answer in faith, “Lord, you are our God.”
classic_reading:
[Hos.2.1-Hos.2.5]
Chapter 2
The idolatry of the people. (Hos. 2:1-5) God's judgments against them. (Hos. 2:6-13) His promises of reconciliation. (Hos. 2:14-23)
Verses 1-5 This chapter continues the figurative address to Israel, in reference to Hosea's wife and children. Let us own and love as brethren, all whom the Lord seems to put among his children, and encourage them in that they have received mercy. But every Christian, by his example and conduct, must protest against evil and abuses, even among those to whom he belongs and owes respect. Impenitent sinners will soon be stripped of the advantages they misuse, and which they consume upon their lusts.
[Hos.2.6-Hos.2.13]
Verses 6-13 God threatens what he would do with this treacherous, idolatrous people. They did not turn, therefore all this came upon them; and it is written for admonition to us. If lesser difficulties be got over, God will raise greater. The most resolute in sinful pursuits, are commonly most crossed in them. The way of God and duty is often hedged about with thorns, but we have reason to think it is a sinful way that is hedged up with thorns. Crosses and obstacles in an evil course are great blessings, and are to be so accounted; they are God's hedges, to keep us from transgressing, to make the way of sin difficult, and to keep us from it. We have reason to bless God for restraining grace, and for restraining providences; and even for sore pain, sickness, or calamity, if it keeps us from sin. The disappointments we meet with in seeking for satisfaction from the creature, should, if nothing else will do it, drive us to the Creator. When men forget, or consider not that their comforts come from God, he will often in mercy take them away, to bring them to think upon their folly and danger. Sin and mirth can never hold long together; but if men will not take away sin from their mirth, God will take away mirth from their sin. And if men destroy God's word and ordinances, it is just with him to destroy their vines and fig-trees. This shall be the ruin of their mirth. Taking away the solemn seasons and the sabbaths will not do it, they will readily part with them, and think it no loss; but He will take away their sensual pleasures. Days of sinful mirth must be visited with days of mourning.
[Hos.2.14-Hos.2.23]
Verses 14-23 After these judgments the Lord would deal with Israel more gently. By the promise of rest in Christ we are invited to take his yoke upon us; and the work of conversion may be forwarded by comforts as well as by convictions. But usually the Lord drives us to despair of earthly joy, and help from ourselves, that, being shut from every other door, we may knock at Mercy's gate. From that time Israel would be more truly attached to the Lord; no longer calling him Baali, or "My lord and master," alluding to authority, rather than love, but Ishi, an address of affection. This may foretell the restoration from the Babylonish captivity; and also be applied to the conversion of the Jews to Christ, in the days of the apostles, and the future general conversion of that nation; and believers are enabled to expect infinitely more tenderness and kindness from their holy God, than a beloved wife can expect from the kindest husband. When the people were weaned from idols, and loved the Lord, no creature should do them any harm. This may be understood of the blessings and privileges of the spiritual Israel, of every true believer, and their partaking of Christ's righteousness; also, of the conversion of the Jews to Christ. Here is an argument for us to walk so that God may not be dishonoured by us: Thou art my people. If a man's family walk disorderly, it is a dishonour to the master. If God call us children, we may say, Thou art our God. Unbelieving soul, lay aside discouraging thoughts; do not thus answer God's loving-kindness. Doth God say, Thou art my people? Say, Lord, thou art our God.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The prophet enters into a new contract, representing the gracious manner in which God will again restore Israel under a new covenant.

God's gracious covenant represented (verses 1–3)

People often dislike true religion because they prefer objects and forms of worship that allow them to indulge their sinful desires instead of putting those desires to death.

How remarkable that a holy God should show goodwill toward people whose sinful minds are hostile to him!

Hosea's actions picture God's gracious dealings with humanity after it departed from him.

They illustrate the covenant of grace he is willing to make with his people:

They will belong to him as his people, and he will be their God.

They must acknowledge the consequences of their wrongdoing and must not return to folly.

One sign that affliction is producing good in us is that we are kept from yielding to the temptations that come with suffering.

Israel's waiting and eventual restoration (verses 4–5)

Here the meaning of the prophetic picture is applied directly to Israel.

The people would remain for a long time like a widow, deprived of joys and honors.

In the end, however, they would be received again.

Those who seek the Lord so as to find him must come to Christ and willingly become his people.

We should fear not only the Lord's greatness, but also his goodness.

We should reverence not only his majesty, but also his mercy.

Henry notes that even Jewish writers apply this passage to the promised Messiah.

He understands it as predicting a future conversion of Jewish people to Christ, for which, in his reading, they have been preserved as a distinct people.

Fear of God may first arise from knowing his holiness and just judgment.

But experiencing mercy and grace through Jesus Christ leads the heart to reverence a loving and glorious Friend and Father and to fear offending him.
classic_reading:
[Hos.3.1-Hos.3.3]
Chapter 3
The prophet enters into a new contract, representing the gracious manner in which God will again restore Israel under a new covenant.
Verses 1-3 The dislike of men to true religion is because they love objects and forms, which allow them to indulge, instead of mortifying their lusts. How wonderful that a holy God should have good-will to those whose carnal mind is enmity against Him! Here is represented God's gracious dealings with the fallen race of mankind, that had gone from him. This is the covenant of grace he is willing to enter into with them, they must be to him a people, and he will be to them a God. They must accept the punishment of their sin, and must not return to folly. And it is a certain sign that our afflictions are means of good to us, when we are kept from being overcome by the temptations of an afflicted state.
[Hos.3.4-Hos.3.5]
Verses 4-5 Here is the application of the parable to Israel. They must long sit like a widow, stripped of all joys and honours; but shall at length be received again. Those that would seek the Lord so as to find him, must apply to Christ, and become his willing people. Not only are we to fear the Lord and his greatness, but the Lord and his goodness; not only his majesty, but his mercy. Even Jewish writers apply this passage to the promised Messiah; doubtless it foretold their future conversion to Christ, for which they are kept a separate people. Though the first fear of God arise from a view of his holy majesty and righteous vengeance, yet the experience of mercy and grace through Jesus Christ, will lead the heart to reverence so kind and glorious a Friend and Father, and to fear offending him.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's judgments against the sins of the people.1–5and of the priests.6–11Idolatry is reproved, and Judah is admonished.12–19
The sins of the people (verses 1–5)

Hosea condemned immorality as well as idolatry.

Truth, mercy and knowledge of God had disappeared from the land.

Violence and murder filled it, as Henry also recalls in 2 Kings 21:16.

Disaster was approaching and would leave the country desolate.

Our sins—whether committed as individuals, families, neighbors or nations—give the Lord cause to bring charges against us.

We should therefore submit to him and humble ourselves, lest his judgments continue toward destruction.

Priests and people reject God's knowledge (verses 6–11)

Both priests and people had rejected the knowledge of God.

God would therefore justly reject them.

They forgot his law.

They neither desired nor tried to keep it in mind or teach it to their descendants.

Therefore God would forget them and their children.

When we use for dishonor the gifts that ought to bring honor to God, those very gifts may become our shame.

The sacrifices should have warned people how seriously God regards sin: atonement was needed.

Instead, the priests encouraged sin by treating its remedy as cheap and easy.

It is wicked to be pleased with other people's wrongdoing because we expect to profit from it.

Gains acquired unlawfully cannot be enjoyed with a peaceful conscience.

Priests and people strengthened one another in wickedness, so they would share the consequences.

Those who share in sin should expect to share its ruin.

A secret sinful desire allowed to remain in the heart can gradually destroy its spiritual strength.

That explains why many professing believers become dull, lifeless and sluggish in serving God.

Some hidden desire has taken hold of their hearts.

Idolatry and God's warning to Judah (verses 12–19)

The people consulted idols instead of God's word.

That led to disorder and sin.

In doing so, they prepared punishments for themselves and helped wrongdoing spread through the nation.

Judah must not imitate Israel's idolatry.

Israel had surrendered itself to false worship and now faced the dreadful command “Leave them alone.”

When people cast off the gentle yoke of Christ, they may continue sinning until God abandons them to their chosen path.

They then receive no further warnings and feel no conviction.

Satan takes hold of them, and they move toward destruction.

Being left undisturbed in sin is a severe divine judgment.

Those who face no disturbance over their sin may ultimately be destroyed because of it.

May God keep us from that dreadful state.

His judgment, like a powerful storm, will soon carry hardened sinners toward ruin.
classic_reading:
[Hos.4.1-Hos.4.5]
Chapter 4
God's judgments against the sins of the people. (Hos. 4:1-5) and of the priests. (Hos. 4:6-11) Idolatry is reproved, and Judah is admonished. (Hos. 4:12-19)
Verses 1-5 Hosea reproves for immorality, as well as idolatry. There was no truth, mercy, or knowledge of God in the land: it was full of murders, II Kin. 21:16. Therefore calamities were near, which would desolate the country. Our sins, as separate persons, as a family, as a neighbourhood, as a nation, cause the Lord to have a controversy with us; let us submit and humble ourselves before Him, that he may not go on to destroy.
[Hos.4.6-Hos.4.11]
Verses 6-11 Both priests and people rejected knowledge; God will justly reject them. They forgot the law of God, neither desired nor endeavoured to retain it in mind, and to transmit the remembrance to their posterity; therefore God will justly forget them and their children. If we dishonour God with that which is our honour, it will, sooner or later, be turned into shame to us. Instead of warning the people against sin, from the consideration of the sacrifices, which showed what an offence sin was to God, since it needed an atonement, the priests encouraged the people to sin, since atonement might be made at so small an expense. It is very wicked to be pleased with the sins of others, because they may turn to our advantage. What is unlawfully gained, cannot be comfortably used. The people and the priests hardened one another in sin; therefore justly shall they share in the punishment. Sharers in sin must expect to share in ruin. Any lust harboured in the heart, in time will eat out all its strength and vigour. That is the reason why many professors grow so heavy, so dull, so dead in the way of religion. They have a liking for some secret lust, which takes away their hearts.
[Hos.4.12-Hos.4.19]
Verses 12-19 The people consulted images, and not the Divine word. This would lead to disorder and sin. Thus men prepare scourges for themselves, and vice is spread through a people. Let not Judah come near the idolatrous worship of Israel. For Israel was devoted to idols, and must now be let alone. When sinners cast off the easy yoke of Christ, they go on in sin till the Lord saith, Let them alone. Then they receive no more warnings, feel no more convictions: Satan takes full possession of them, and they ripen for destruction. It is a sad and sore judgment for any man to be let alone in sin. Those who are not disturbed in their sin, will be destroyed for their sin. May we be kept from this awful state; for the wrath of God, like a strong tempest, will soon hurry impenitent sinners into ruin.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Divine judgments against Israel.1–7Approaching desolations threatened.8–15
The Lord exposes Israel's hidden sins (verses 1–7)

God's searching eyes saw Israel's secret attachment to sin, the people's love for their wrong practices and the power those practices exercised over them.

Pride makes people stubborn in every other sin.

Judah was following the same path and would therefore fall with Israel.

People who deal falsely with the Lord are only deceiving themselves.

Those who seek God merely by bringing flocks and herds, while withholding their hearts and souls, cannot expect to find him.

Those who do not seek the Lord while he may be found will not succeed later.

It is therefore vital to seek him now, in the accepted time and day of salvation.

Judgment approaches, but repentance remains possible (verses 8–15)

The destruction announced to unrepentant sinners is not merely a warning intended to frighten them.

It is a sentence that will not be recalled if they refuse to repent.

That we receive timely warning is itself a mercy, allowing us to flee from coming judgment.

Following human commands that contradict God's commands prepares a people for ruin.

Sometimes God's judgments consume sinful people like a moth, dry rot or woodworm.

The damage proceeds quietly.

People may imagine themselves secure and prosperous, only to discover later that everything has been gradually decaying.

God often allows this process to unfold slowly to give them time to repent.

A nation, like an individual, can waste away by degrees.

Lesser judgments are sent to warn sinners and prevent greater calamities if they will listen.

When Israel and Judah were threatened, they sought protection from Assyria.

This only made their injury worse.

Affliction would eventually drive them to seek God himself.

There is hope when people begin to grieve more deeply over their sins than over their suffering.

Under conviction and correction, we should seek to know the Lord.

Those led by severe trials to seek him genuinely will find him an immediate helper and a secure refuge.

With him there is abundant redemption for everyone who calls upon him.

True, lasting peace is found only where God is.
classic_reading:
[Hos.5.1-Hos.5.7]
Chapter 5
The Divine judgments against Israel. (Hos. 5:1-7) Approaching desolations threatened. (Hos. 5:8-15)
Verses 1-7 The piercing eye of God saw secret liking and disposition to sin, the love the house of Israel had to their sins, and the dominion their sins had over them. Pride makes men obstinate in other sins. And as Judah was treading in the same steps, they would fall with Israel. By dealing treacherously with the Lord, men only deceive themselves. Those that go to seek the Lord with their flocks and their herds only, and not with their hearts and souls, cannot expect to find him; nor shall any speed who do not seek the Lord while he may be found. See how much it is our concern to seek God early, now, while it is the accepted time, and the day of salvation.
[Hos.5.8-Hos.5.15]
Verses 8-15 The destruction of impenitent sinners is not mere talk, to frighten them, it is a sentence which will not be recalled. And it is a mercy that we have timely warning given us, that we may flee from the wrath to come. Compliance with the commandments of men, who thwart the commandments of God, ripens a people for ruin. The judgments of God are sometimes to a sinful people as a moth, and as rottenness, or as a worm; as these consume the clothes and the wood, so shall the judgments of God consume them. Silently, they shall think themselves safe and thriving, but when they look into their state, shall find themselves wasting and decaying. Slowly, for the Lord gives them space to repent. Many a nation; as well as many a person, dies of a consumption. Gradually, God comes upon sinners with lesser judgments, to prevent greater, if they will be wise, and take warning. When Israel and Judah found themselves in danger, they sought the protection of the Assyrians, but this only helped to make their wound the worse. They would be forced to apply to God. He will bring them home to himself, by afflictions. When men begin to complain more of their sins than of their afflictions, then there begins to be some hope of them; and when under the conviction of sin, and the corrections of the rod, we must seek the knowledge of God. Those who are led by severe trials to seek God earnestly and sincerely, will find him a present help and an effectual refuge; for with him is plenteous redemption for all who call upon him. There is solid peace, and there only, where God is.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesAn exhortation to repentance.1–3Israel's instability and breach of the covenant.4–11
Return to the Lord (verses 1–3)

People who joined together to abandon God and draw one another into sin should join together to return to him.

That will bring glory to God and good to themselves.

During suffering, we are strengthened and encouraged to repent by maintaining right thoughts about God's goodness and purposes.

Deliverance from distress can be like life restored from death.

God promises to revive his people, and the assurance of his mercy should draw them back.

Henry also sees a further reference here to the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

He marvels that a prophecy concerning the church's deliverance would point toward salvation through Christ.

In his reading, the resurrection confirms that Jesus is the promised One and that believers need no other Savior.

The promised blessing is eternal life through knowing God.

God's returning favor is as certain as morning following a dark night.

He comes like the early and late rain, refreshing the ground and making it fruitful.

The grace of God in Christ is both rains: it begins and sustains the work of spiritual fruitfulness.

Just as the Redeemer rose from the grave, he will revive the hearts and hopes of everyone who trusts him.

Even a small ray of hope from God's word promises increasing light, comfort, cleansing and fruitful grace.

Israel's passing repentance (verses 4–11)

Under suffering, Israel and Judah sometimes appeared willing to repent.

But their apparent goodness vanished like a morning cloud or early dew.

They soon returned to their former corruption.

That is why the Lord sent such serious warnings through his prophets.

God's word will be the death either of sin or of the sinner.

The Lord desires mercy rather than sacrifice and knowledge of himself that produces holy reverence and love.

This exposes the folly of people who trust external religious ceremonies to compensate for lack of love toward God and other people.

As Adam broke God's covenant in paradise, so Israel broke its national covenant despite the many blessings it had received.

Judah too had become ready for judgment.

May the Lord establish his reverence and kingdom within our hearts, never abandon us to ourselves and not permit temptation to overcome us.
classic_reading:
[Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3]
Chapter 6
An exhortation to repentance. (Hos. 6:1-3) Israel's instability and breach of the covenant. (Hos. 6:4-11)
Verses 1-3 Those who have gone from God by consent, and in a body, drawing one another to sin, should, by consent and in a body, return to him, which will be for his glory, and their good. It will be of great use for support under afflictions, and to encourage our repentance, to keep up good thoughts of God, and of his purposes and designs concerning us. Deliverance out of trouble should be to them as life from the dead. God will revive them: the assurance of this should engage them to return to him. But this seems to have a further reference to the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Let us admire the wisdom and goodness of God, that when the prophet foretold the deliverance of the church out of her troubles, he should point out our salvation by Christ; and now these words are fulfilled in the resurrection of Christ, it confirms our faith, that this is He that should come and we are to look for no other. Here is a precious blessing promised; this is life eternal, to know God. The returns of the favour of God are secured to us as firmly as the return of the morning after a dark night. He shall come to us as the latter and former rain unto the earth, which refreshes it, and makes it fruitful. The grace of God in Christ is both the latter and the former rain; and by it the good work of our fruit-bearing is begun and carried on. And as the Redeemer was raised from the grave, so will He revive the hearts and hopes of all that trust in him. The feeblest glimpse of hope in his word, is a sure earnest of increasing light and comfort, which shall be attended with purifying, comforting grace that makes fruitful.
[Hos.6.4-Hos.6.11]
Verses 4-11 Sometimes Israel and Judah seemed disposed to repent under their sufferings, but their goodness vanished like the empty morning cloud, and the early dew, and they were as vile as ever. Therefore the Lord sent awful messages by the prophets. The word of God will be the death either of the sin or of the sinner. God desired mercy rather than sacrifice, and that knowledge of him which produces holy fear and love. This exposes the folly of those who trust in outward observances, to make up for their want of love to God and man. As Adam broke the covenant of God in paradise, so Israel had broken his national covenant, notwithstanding all the favours they received. Judah also was ripe for Divine judgments. May the Lord put his fear into our hearts, and set up his kingdom within us, and never leave us to ourselves, nor suffer us to be overcome by temptation.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe manifold sins of Israel.1–7Their senselessness and hypocrisy.8–16
Israel's many sins (verses 1–7)

Israel's wickedness arose from a practical refusal to believe that God governs and sees human affairs.

The people acted as though he neither saw their sins nor cared about them.

Their wrongdoing surrounded them.

Their hearts were inflamed by sinful desires like a blazing oven.

Even when the nation was in trouble, they never thought to seek God's help.

The visible acts of sin in a person's life are only a small part of the evil within the heart.

When a sinful desire is deliberately cherished inwardly, it eventually breaks out into actual wrongdoing.

Those who tempt others into drunkenness cannot be true friends.

They often intend the other person's ruin.

Thus people become instruments of judgment against one another.

Those who continue living without prayer even during danger and distress are not merely heated with sin; they have become hardened in it.

Israel's instability and hypocrisy (verses 8–16)

Israel resembled a cake not turned over: burned on one side and still raw on the other, useless throughout.

The nation mixed the worship of Jehovah with idolatry.

Signs of approaching destruction had appeared, like gray hair announcing age, yet Israel did not notice them.

The pride that moves people to break God's law also encourages self-flattery.

God's mercy and grace are the only safe refuge, but stubborn sinners seldom think of fleeing there.

They may cry out in fear with words resembling prayer, but their hearts do not truly turn to God.

Even requests for earthly blessings may aim only to provide more fuel for sinful pleasures.

Changing from one religious group, opinion, outward form or particular vice to another still leaves people far from Christ and genuine holiness.

This is what we are like by nature, and what we will become if left to ourselves.

Let us therefore pray:

Create a clean heart in us, O God, and renew a right spirit within us.

Israel's empty claim to know God (verses 1–4)

When Israel faced disaster, the people would claim to know God and ask for his protection.

But such words would be disregarded.

What good is it to say “My God, I know you” if we cannot also say “My God, I love you, serve you and cling to you alone”?

Idolatry produces a barren harvest (verses 5–10)

By worshiping idols, the people promised themselves abundance, peace and military success.

Those expectations would come to nothing.

They sowed seed that produced no stalk or blade.

Even if a shoot appeared, it would produce no grain.

The works of darkness are barren, and their final outcome is death.

The hopes of sinners will deceive them, while the gains they seek become traps.

In times of danger—and especially at the final judgment—every merely human or worldly strategy will fail.

The people chose to go their own way.

Like a solitary wild donkey, they became easier prey for a lion.

Human beings most resemble an untamed donkey when they seek from created things the help and fulfillment that come only from God.

Sinners may experience some sorrow.

But if it is not godly sorrow leading to repentance, it will end in lasting grief.

Corrupt worship cannot make up for disobedience (verses 11–14)

To corrupt the worship of God is a serious sin, regardless of how reasonable the excuses may appear.

The Lord had caused his law to be written down for Israel.

Yet the people neither wanted to know it nor intended to obey.

They built temples as though they remembered their Creator, but had actually forgotten him because they no longer feared him.

No one has hardened the heart against God and ultimately prospered.

As long as people despise the truths, commands and appointed worship of Scripture, elaborate and costly ceremonies of their own invention only increase their guilt.

Only worship performed according to God's word and through Jesus Christ is acceptable to him.

So long as men despise the truths and precepts of God's word, and the ordinances of his worship, all the observances and offerings, however costly, of their own devising, will be unto them for sin; for those services only are acceptable to God, which are done according to his word, and through Jesus Christ.

Israel's misplaced joy will end (verses 1–6)

Israel offered gifts to its idols.

People who are stingy about true worship may spend lavishly on their own sinful desires.

Anyone who values the harvest floor's reward more highly than God's favor and eternal life is, in that sense, an idolater.

The people rejoiced over their harvest while having no desire to grieve over sin.

When we make the world and its possessions our idol and our portion, God is just in exposing our folly and correcting us.

Those who refuse God's laws and his love cannot expect to enjoy the Lord's land as though nothing were wrong.

When we possess the means of grace, we should ask how we would live if those gifts were removed.

The joy of fellowship with God remains secure amid earthly change.

But pleasant homes and properties bought or protected with money may be destroyed.

No famine is more dreadful than a famine of the soul.

The appointed watchmen become traps (verses 7–10)

There had been a time when Israel's spiritual watchmen walked with God.

Now they acted like a birdcatcher's snare, trapping people and bringing them toward ruin.

The people's corruption resembled that of Gibeah (Judges 19).

Their crimes would bring comparable judgment.

At first, God had found Israel delightful, like grapes discovered by a traveler in the wilderness, or the first ripe figs of the season.

These pictures show how much pleasure God had taken in his people.

Nevertheless, they abandoned him and followed idols.

Judgment reaches Israel's comforts and descendants (verses 11–17)

God departs from a person or people when he withdraws his goodness and mercy.

When the Lord has withdrawn, what can created things accomplish?

Outward comforts may remain for a time, but the true blessing is gone when God is gone.

Children as well as parents would suffer.

God's wrath dries the roots and withers the fruit of worldly comforts.

Henry points to the continued scattering of the Jewish people in his own era as a warning not to neglect or abuse gospel privileges.

Yet not every painful blow means that God is drying up the root.

Sometimes he strikes a plant so that its sap goes deeper into the root, producing greater humility, patience, faith and self-denial.

God is just when he judges people who despise the mercy he offers.

The distress to come upon Israel. (Hos. 9:1-6) The approach of the day of trouble. (Hos. 9:7-10) Judgments on Israel. (Hos. 9:11-17)
Verses 1-6 Israel gave rewards to their idols, in the offerings presented to them. It is common for those who are niggardly in religion, to be prodigal upon their lusts. Those are reckoned as idolaters, who love a reward in the corn-floor better than a reward in the favour of God and in eternal life. They are full of the joy of harvest, and have no disposition to mourn for sin. When we make the world, and the things of it, our idol and our portion, it is just with God to show us our folly, and correct us. None may expect to dwell in the Lord's land, who will not be subject to the Lord's laws, or be influenced by his love. When we enjoy the means of grace, we ought to consider what we shall do, if they should be taken from us. While the pleasures of communion with God are out of the reach of change, the pleasant places purchased with silver, or in which men deposit silver, are liable to be laid in ruins. No famine is so dreadful as that of the soul.
[Hos.9.7-Hos.9.10]
Verses 7-10 Time had been when the spiritual watchmen of Israel were with the Lord, but now they were like the snare of a fowler to entangle persons to their ruin. The people were become as corrupt as those of Gibeah, Judg. 19; and their crimes should be visited in like manner. At first God had found Israel pleasing to Him, as grapes to the traveller in the wilderness. He saw them with pleasure as the first ripe figs. This shows the delight God took in them; yet they followed after idolatry.
[Hos.9.11-Hos.9.17]
Verses 11-17 . God departs from a people, or from a person, when he withdraws his goodness and mercy from them; and when the Lord is departed, what can the creature do? Even though, for the present, good things seem to remain, yet the blessing is gone if God is gone. Even the children should perish with the parents. The Divine wrath dries up the root, and withers the fruit of all comforts; and the scattered Jews daily warn us to beware, lest we neglect or abuse the gospel. Yet every smiting is not a drying up of the root. It may be that God intends only to smite so that the sap may be turned to the root, that there may be more of root graces, more humility, patience, faith, and self-denial. It is very just that God should bring judgments on those who slight his offered mercy.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe idolatry of Israel.1–8They are exhorted to repentance.9–15
Israel is a vine without good fruit (verses 1–8)

A vine's value lies in the fruit it produces.

Israel, however, had brought none of its fruit to maturity.

The people's hearts were divided.

God is the rightful sovereign of the human heart: he requires the whole heart, not merely a share.

If our hearts were directed wholly toward God, devotion would flow strongly enough to overcome whatever lay in its path.

Israel's claims to be in covenant with God were false.

Even its administration of justice had become as poisonous as hemlock.

How sad that the visible church may still be a nearly empty vine!

Earthly prosperity is no more substantial than bubbles or foam on water, quickly broken and gone.

Sinners will one day seek shelter in vain from the very Judge they now despise when he is offered to them as Savior.

Seek the Lord and sow righteousness (verses 9–15)

God does not delight in sinners' death and destruction.

For that reason, his correction can be an act of mercy.

Sinful habits remained deeply rooted in Israel.

Enemies would gather against the people.

It is just for those who live carelessly in comfort and indulgence to learn what suffering means.

They should cleanse their hearts of sinful loves and desires and become brokenhearted and contrite.

They should abound in devotion toward God and in justice and generosity toward one another.

This is what it means to sow to the Spirit.

Seeking the Lord is a duty for every day, though there are special occasions that call us to seek him with renewed urgency.

Christ will come as the Lord our righteousness, granting his righteousness abundantly.

Those who sow righteousness reap according to mercy.

Such a harvest is a reward of grace, not a debt God owes us.

Even the profits obtained through sin bring sinners no real satisfaction.

Both sinful comforts and confidence in wicked practices will eventually disappoint.

Come, seek the Lord: hope placed in him will not deceive you.

Consider the cruelty and devastation of war.

Whatever evil is done, sin lies behind it.

How much misery human wrongdoing brings even in this life!

Verses 1-8 A vine is only valuable for its fruit; but Israel now brought no fruit to perfection. Their hearts were divided. God is the Sovereign of the heart; he will have all, or none. Were the stream of the heart wholly after God, it would run strongly, and bear down all before it. Their pretences to covenant with God were false. Even the proceeding of justice was as poisonous hemlock. Alas, how empty a vine is the visible church even at this day! But all earthly prosperity is but a collection of bubbles, soon destroyed like foam upon the water. Sinners will in vain seek shelter from that Judge, whom they now despise as a Saviour.
[Hos.10.9-Hos.10.15]
Verses 9-15 Because God does not desire the death and ruin of sinners, therefore in mercy he desires their chastisement. The children of iniquity still remained in Israel. The enemies would be gathered against them. It is just with God to make those know what hardships mean, who indulge themselves in ease and pleasure. Let them cleanse their hearts from all corrupt affections and lusts, and be a broken and contrite spirit. Let them abound in works of piety towards God, and of justice and charity towards one another: herein let them sow to the Spirit. Seeking the Lord is to be every day's work, but there are special occasions when to seek him. Christ shall come as the Lord our righteousness, and grant us of it abundantly. If we sow in righteousness, we shall reap according to mercy; a reward not of debt, but of grace. Even the gains of sin yield the sinner no satisfaction. As our comforts, so our confidences in the service of sin will certainly fail us. Come and seek the Lord, and thy hope in him shall not deceive thee. See what cruel work war makes. Whatever mischief is done, it is sin that does it. What miseries men's sins bring on them, even in this world!
